review_text: Dr. Yoon's delightful attitude towards student concerns was not enough to fully recommend him as a lecturer. This course is pretty dry and dull in terms of material, so I am not sure if any other teacher would've made it more interesting for me, but Dr. Yoon certainly did not. I took this course during a summer session so it was compacted into classes every day for 6 weeks. We had one midterm exam, a home work every week and a final exam. I felt so inadequately prepared for both exams, and the homeworks were tedious busy work. On top of that he assigned a coding project in C that was a simulation of the MIPS pipeline process (You learn about this during the class) and it was the second hardest project I ever took on and I felt it was just useless busy work. The midterm was incredibly long and ridiculously packed with material not many were familiar with. He even said he anticipated low exam scores because people would not finish on time. For the first exam, we originally had 85 minutes, however since there was no class after ours let out he extended it to 100 minutes because people needed more time. This was the same situation for the final exam only no time extension. I barely got time to go to all the questions and just attempt them. The one thing that makes this class with Yoon worth it, is it can be a passable class since he gives a butt load of extra credit and partial credit for just attempting questions but not necessarily answering them correctly. Because of the unreasonable amount of questions on exams, the difficulty of the project and homeworks, the average of the class was a 56%. So Yoon curved the course NICELY. I ended up with a 66% and that was good enough for a B- . I like Yoon as a person and he's very helpful in his office hours but he still isn't very clear on the material a lot of times. Since I do not know how the other teachers are for 411 I cannot suggest taking them over Yoon. If you have to take Yoon just remember these things 1) The exams are unreasonably long and nearly impossible to get an A on, but he gives a lot of partial credit for simply attempting questions. 2) The project he assigns is hard and unnecessary busy work. 3) He isn't very effective as a lecturer, and does not give enough resources and practice materials to prepare you for exams. Even homeworks are not sufficient.

The homework is time-consuming/difficult and the exams are challenging. review_text: As a person he's a great guy. As a teacher, there is much left to be desired. Most of the content you will learn are asynchronous which makes lectures either redundant or near useless 9 times out of 10. But you can't just not show up to lecture, there are graded in class group activities which are also useless and I'm 99% sure you could pass comfortably with an A even if you didn't get those points. There are times where an actual new or interesting concept will be introduced in lecture but more often than not you will walk away wondering what you actually learned in that 50 minute period. As for coursework the bulk of the grade comes from 4 exams, one of which is dropped. Most of them are relatively easy if you have any programming experience at all but there's a few questions that are about very specific techniques in python. The 3 homeworks throughout the semester are sort of the projects you would expect of a programming course which aside from the final project are the most time consuming. But even then if you have any programming experience at all you could finish one in 1 or 2 hours and you have unlimited attempts so you can just keep debugging and resubmitting until you check all the boxes which is nice. Considering this is the main programming course of the info sci major, I can't say this course had the rigor I expected. Maybe that sounds great to some of you but if you're expecting a programming course that has any difficulty then this is not it. Even the final project felt like a softball and the hardest part was getting your group members to commit and push to github. Most of the other assignments are just you explaining certain concepts in your own words and then provide working examples yourself which I find would be unhelpful to anyone learning python for the first time. And everyone else talking about the grading is not making it up. I kid you not, I waited until a few days before final grades were due and I got everything graded all at once in the span of an hour. So don't expect to get any grades back throughout the semester or know what your grade is at all. review_text: Before I get into my review, I should note that the C+ is pretty much entirely on me. I should have taken the course more seriously, especially for the first midterm, and I got burned for not doing so. At least I passed. With that said, this class did not work for me whatsoever. It's not because the class is hard, though it absolutely is, and I'd argue it should be. I just don't think it's for the right reasons. For instance, the lecture/exam half of the course is almost entirely disjoint from the GeekOS project half of the course, and it really feels like a 5/6 credit course sometimes. Being good at the lecture content will not help you whatsoever with GeekOS, and vice versa. This seems to be a 412-wide issue. Regarding the lecture content, I don't think Pete is a very good lecturer. It's sort of what the other reviewers this semester so far have pointed out. I wouldn't quite agree with the tin can rattling mentality, but he certainly doesn't practice his presentations, and he brings absolutely no energy to the class. Another reviewer pointed out the ChatGPT image, which he said he would fix and never did, but there was another instance where he took a TRIO slide set from the internet, didn't review it at all beforehand, and tried going through it in a rather miserable showing. There's very little transformation of his slide content in his lectures, as all he does is take his laser pointer and point to things he wants to emphasize on one of the projectors in the room. The slides themselves are rather poor summaries of OSTEP, which he follows very closely. That's just lectures themselves. The assignments he gives aren't much better in my opinion. He assigns weekly Gradescope reading homeworks which are worth 1% of the grade each. I honestly almost wish he would give more traditional homeworks instead. Some of the questions are horribly ambiguous, there's no room to state any assumptions, there are some questions where it feels like even with both the slides and OSTEP you can't really answer well, they ultimately lack engagement, and they are nowhere near comprehensive enough to actually prepare for the exams imo. Regarding exams, exam 1 was insane with the short answer questions of random topics from the slides being worth so much of the grade, while exams 2 and 3, especially 3, were relatively more chill. These certainly weren't my strongsuit, as I'm horrible with memorizing topics which I haven't worked directly with in some meaningful way, and I'm rather terrible at studying. I didn't like them, but they were fine I guess. One question I would like to address is the barber shop semaphore problem in exam 2. Not only were the semantics poorly defined, as the professor admitted, but in my experience, semaphore programming isn't just something just I get right away. I haven't worked with them before, as I haven't had any need to. They really weren't gone over well in class, nor were the gradescope assignments enough to really nail it in. He didn't give any other practice problem on them besides the baboon problem from a reading homework. I realize this is just one specific example, but it's emblematic of my problem with this part of the class as a whole. I also realize this could just be me, and my review should be taken with at least a grain of salt due to my meager performance compared to the rest of the class. I didn't mention this before, but each exam was 15%, and there was no final exam. Regarding GeekOS, the TA's, especially Leo, really carried here. They were really helpful in getting some of the projects working, and I really wouldn't have passed the class without them. Though, I'd maybe argue they were a bit too necessary to get through the projects. It's very clear the project specs haven't been updated in years, and the project slides, especially for the later projects such as 4b and all of 5, don't seem at all sufficient in getting you through the projects. Of course, the projects should be challenging, but in my experience, there was a lot of frustration due to how much information the slides and specs omit. For example, in project 5, file systems, GFS3 is a completely proprietary file system, yet we're not really given a good specification of it. For example, we were only given one example GFS3 image whose structure is completely undocumented. In project 4b, demand paging (the hardest project imo, though I hated 5 more just by nature), the way in which we were basically required to do things isn't very easy to deduce from source code, and the slides honestly made it more confusing what we had to do. Don't get me wrong, these projects are pretty cool at the end of the day, and honestly it was very useful being forced to navigate and implement significant components into a Linux-like kernel. I just think the projects would be better if the provided resources were more helpful. Finally, there's grading. The class is graded on a curve. This semester, seemingly a lot of insanely smart people took the class, which seemingly skewed the grade distribution like crazy. There was a review last semester of someone getting an 88 with Dr. Agrawala and ending with an A+. I know someone who got like an 89 this semester and ended with an A-. Take that for what you will. Overall, I can't say I don't recommend taking this class at all, but I have some issues with it. Pete is teaching this class next spring, so it seems for a little bit, Dr. Agrawala and Pete are alternating teaching this class.

review_text: I'd give 4.7 stars if PlanetTerp had such an option. This is a hard class. Not in the way that MATH140/141 are considered "hard", or in the way that Kruskal's classes are "hard" (at least his 351), but rather it is hard by virtue of the material. Algorithms are just often difficult concepts to grasp and really understand to the depth that Childs' wants his students to be able to grasp and understand for his assignments and exams. The class is paced quite nicely for me - I showed up to every lecture, and I feel like I gained something from each one. I was able to ask questions pretty frequently (perhaps too frequently), and Childs' would always spend the time to think about an answer to each one, and I felt that that helped me understand the material greatly. He records all of his lectures and posts all of his notes. The only things from class not available asynchronously online are the Q&A times that he holds in the 5-10 minutes before each class begins. The assignments are hard. (Did I mention the class is hard?) The first two took me about 10 hours each, and the other three 15-20 hours each. Each one is a set of five problems, the answers to which require (unless you're a super-mega-genius I guess) intuition and material from the lectures. A quote from one of his office hours: "If you're stuck on this problem, think about the algorithms we covered in class; I make the homeworks directly related [to those]." - Childs My strategy for the homeworks were to look at the problems when they were assigned, then keep them in mind over the next two weeks of lectures (each assignment is assigned exactly two weeks before they're due). Spending the time to actually understand the material on them is definitely helpful - they're actually harder than the exam questions by a solid margin, and they mirror the exam structure. Also, he drops the lowest of the five assignments, so each of your best four assignments comprise 10% of your final grade. Considering that there is ample time for each one, it's definitely possible to have the assignments be the grade fallback. The exams are hard. (yes.) The midterm is worth 20% of your final grade, and the final 40%. There's definitely a time-crunch aspect to this. As of writing this review, I haven't taken the final yet. But speaking from the midterm experience, there wasn't a single student that left the exam room early (shocker). Although it seemed like most of the class felt pretty bad about the midterm, to Childs', the midterm was "on the easier side." (Avg 69, median 70 iirc) I did well enough not to have major complaints about it, and other reviews go more in-depth. The textbook is... something that I didn't read. I'm sure it was useful to those who did, but the lectures + questions + office hours + assignments prepared me well enough to face the exams. Although Childs' is a great lecturer and all-around smart guy, he's definitely a bit hard to talk to. He feels like a classic computer-focused guy (which is fair, since he's getting paid for it lol), and I definitely agree with the previous reviewer that said it felt impossible to build rapport with him. TL;DR: Great lecturer, fair class, hard af so look at the grade distr. to make your choice
label_rationale: Homework and exams are very difficult and time-intensive, but closely aligned with lectures and described as fair.

review_text: TL;DR - If you want to go into Data Science as a career, then you should take Max. Otherwise, stay far FAR away. Pros: - Everything he teaches is from a practical perspective. He frames the class and his lectures in a way that would actually help someone in the future if they wanted to go into data science. This is something that a lot of CS classes fail to do in high school and college, so finding a course that directly prepares you for a career in the subject area is rare. So as someone who wants to go into Data Sci / AI / ML, this class was incredibly helpful. - He's a fun guy - We got an A on pretty much all of the homework assignments Cons: - The exams were really tough. He makes exams so that all of the questions are open ended and require critical thinking. Because of this, it's hard to figure out what to expect on an exam. He only gave us one practice exam for each of our exams, so there just wasn't that much material to prepare with. It felt like you either knew it or you didn't. - The class and lectures are incredibly disorganized. We had at least 3 lectures where he showed up with an unfinished slideshow. He knows all of the material that he's gonna teach, he just sometimes shows up unprepared to lectures. The class is also disorganized as well. Many assignments were posted days or weeks after they should've been. - None of the assignments had a clear rubric. We were given very little instruction on what we should actually be doing for some of assignments. This led to a lot of late night frustration as we just didn't know what the right answer for a given problem was supposed to be. This was because of how little specification was given for the assignments.
label_rationale: Tough exams, unclear rubrics, late assignments, and disorganized lectures create substantial effort and confusion.

review_text: Cliff runs the most organized class I’ve taken at UMD. Exams, projects, and quizzes were all fair, and I didn’t have any major complaints. His lectures are a bit boring, and his slides are practically useless, but his notes are really good. You should be aware that projects are modified/made from scratch during the semester, so some projects will have important clarifications after their release and the auto-grader is often released well after the project is. I’d definitely recommend taking him.

review_text: If you had Justin for 351 then expect a similar teaching style. Justin handwrites his notes in class and also has his extensive pdf notes online. Lectures are not recorded. There are about 6 coding projects done in Python along with a weekly homework. There are two midterms with the first being in the middle of the semester and the second being near the end. There is also a take-home final. I highly recommend taking this class, especially if it is with Justin, because you get to learn many different useful data structures and Justin is able to teach the concepts and usefulness of the data structures very well. Justin does teach this class to be more mathematical so expect some proofs and calculations but they are fair.

review_text: I agree with the latest reviews, and I really discourage you from taking this course with her. It’s just very bad. Half of the class literally got a D on Midterm 2, and she called it a “solid performance”? OK, let me be honest—half of the class did better on Midterm 1 by getting away with a C-. How is that solid? Maybe there’s something wrong with how the course is being taught and structured. She seems completely unaware of the issues in the class. It's okay with her that half the class is doing well while the other half is failing. This basically means she doesn’t question why 50% of the class is failing. For her, the most important thing is that a small portion of the class does well, and the rest should just be “failures,” which she accepts as normal. I’m not the type of person who doesn’t put in effort and then blames the professor for that. Even in the most difficult core CS classes at UMD, I could get a B+ or higher if I put in a lot of effort. This class, however, is different. You can put in a lot of effort but still get lost when you're taking the exam. The issue might also be with the slides and the lack of practice material. Unfortunately, this semester was super stressful because of this class. I just want to warn others about the potential distress this class can cause, despite your best efforts to learn and perform well.
evidence_snippet: put in a lot of effort but still get lost
label_rationale: The course is highly stressful despite major effort, with difficult exams, weak practice, and poor structure.
